units.translation: The tragic poets use the present κλύω [I hear] and the imperfect ἔκλυον [I heard], with the υ always shortened. The imperatives κλύθι [hear!] and κλῦτε [hear! (pl.)], or with reduplication κέκλυθι [hear!] and κέκλυτε [hear! (pl.)], are frequent in the epic poets, but not in the tragic poets, except that Aeschylus and Sophocles sometimes said κλύθι [hear!] and Aeschylus κλῦτε [hear! (pl.)], and Aeschylus indeed κλῦθι [hear!] at Ch. 139, 332, Eum. 323, Suppl. 347 and κλῦτε [hear! (pl.)] at Ch. 399. The verb is proper to poetic diction, rare in the comic poets, very common in the tragic poets. Its meaning is the same as that of the verb ἀκούω [I hear], audio, whence Aristophanes in Frogs 1174 ridicules Aeschylus, who at Ch. 5 said κλύειν ἀκοῦσαι [to hear to listen], for joining synonymous words: τοῦθ᾽ ἕτερον αὖθις λέγει, κλύειν ἀκοῦσαι, ταὐτὸν ὂν σαφέστατα [he says this other thing again, to hear to listen, which is most clearly the same]. It is used, exactly like ἀκούω [I hear] (on which see p. 15 and 16): 1. bare, without a case. 2. with the genitive or accusative of the thing. 3. with the genitive of the speaker and the accusative of the thing, sometimes with the genitive or accusative of the participle added. 4. with the prepositions πρός [from], ἀπό [from], ἐκ [from]. 5. with the particles ὡς [that] and ὁθούνεκα [because]. When it has the meaning of hearing or obeying, it is constructed only with the genitive. The following are examples of the first meaning, audio or I perceive with my ears.
